project.title: Counting Pairwise Handshakes
project.problem: A group has n people, and each pair shakes hands exactly once. Determine the total number of handshakes for general positive integer n. Justify the counting argument and state clearly whether a person may shake their own hand.

strategies.title: Direct counting
strategies.approach: Count each unordered pair exactly once. Verify the pattern for n = 1, 2, 3, and 4, then explain why the count is the sum 1 + 2 + … + (n − 1).
strategies.summary: A direct bijection between handshakes and two-person subsets.

strategies.title: Double count incidences
strategies.approach: Count person-handshake incidences in two ways. Each of n people participates in n − 1 handshakes, and each handshake contributes two incidences. Equate the totals and check edge cases.
strategies.summary: An independent derivation by counting endpoints.

timeline.message: Both counting arguments agree; boundary cases n = 1 and n = 2 match the stated assumptions.

output.title: Independent derivation check
output.approach: The handshake count is the number of 2-element subsets of the group.
output.evidence_boundary: The finite checks illustrate the formula; the subset-counting argument establishes the general result.

research_quality.label: Verification
research_quality.value: General counting argument; independently derived below

solution_review.claim: The number of handshakes is n(n − 1)/2.
solution_review.argument_summary: Each handshake corresponds to one unordered pair of distinct people, so the total is the binomial coefficient C(n, 2).

strategy_assessments.rationale: The pair-to-handshake correspondence covers every handshake exactly once.

output.claim: For n people, there are n(n − 1)/2 handshakes.
output.method: Choose the first participant in n ways and the second in n − 1 ways. Each pair is counted twice, once in each order, so divide by two.
output.skeptic_response: The ordered-pair count must be divided by two because order does not distinguish a handshake.
objections: The formula gives zero at n = 1; confirm this matches the setup.
output.next_question: Check small cases and provide an independent derivation.

artifacts.claim: The handshake total equals the number of two-person subsets, C(n, 2).
artifacts.method: Bijection: map each handshake to the unordered pair of participants.
artifacts.evidence_status: General combinatorial argument; no external model or execution required.
artifacts.skeptic_response: Each unordered pair participates in exactly one handshake by the problem statement.
artifacts.next_question: Compare with the endpoint double count.

computational_evidence.interpretation: Saved finite check of the formula for n = 1 through 5; this illustrates the result and is not the general proof.
